Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) Second Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan II) (c. 600 AD)

DEATH OF ṢIRUṢAYDAN — narrative climax of the trilogy's PRINCIPAL VILLAIN-ARC that has run from 1 Mq Ch. 1 through 2 Mq Ch. 12 (the MOST EXTENDED SUSTAINED-VILLAIN narrative in the Meqabyan corpus). Ṣiruṣaydan's death pattern echoes the divine-judgment-on-prideful-kings tradition: Nebuchadnezzar at Daniel 4:31-37 (driven to graze like an ox) + Herod at Acts 12:23 (eaten by worms) + Antiochus IV at 2 Maccabees 9 (worm-infested + foul-smelling demise). Per Horovitz 1905 + Dillmann Lexicon Linguae Aethiopicae (1865): Ṣiruṣaydan etymology connects to TYRE + SIDON (Ṣiru + Ṣaydan), the Phoenician-coastal cities + canonical-type for arrogant maritime-commercial power (Ezekiel 26-28 prophecies). The villain-name is itself a TYPOLOGICAL CIPHER rather than historical-king identification.

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) Second Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan II) (c. 600 AD)

SONS-OF-MAQABIS-OF-MOAB CONFRONT ṢIRUṢAYDAN — pre-martyrdom confrontation-speech (vv. 5-9; expands seed 12:11 villain-arc context). The sons' confrontation parallels the standard PROPHET-CONFRONTS-KING pattern (cf. seed 2:1 Re'ay-confronts-Maqabis) but with martyrs-confronting-tyrant: DANIEL 5 (Daniel confronts Belshazzar — 'thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting'); 2 KINGS 1:9-15 (Elijah confronts Ahaziah's captains); JEREMIAH 38:14-28 (Jeremiah confronts Zedekiah in prison); MATTHEW 14:1-12 (John-the-Baptist confronts Herod-Antipas — and is beheaded). Meqabyan's distinctive feature: the confrontation-speech-from-martyr-to-tyrant locates the martyrs in the PROPHETIC-INSTRUCTION genre rather than the passive-suffering-victim genre. The sons function as Daniel-like-prophets in their martyrdom — an aspect that links the 1 Mq + 2 Mq twin-martyrdom-cycles to the Danielic-confrontation tradition.

ṢIRUṢAYDAN'S FOUL-SMELLING DEMISE — the proud-tyrant-pestilence-death topos (paired with seed 12:11 villain-arc climax). The death-by-foul-disease pattern parallels: 2 MACCABEES 9:5-12 (Antiochus IV's worm-infested-and-foul-smelling demise — the canonical-LXX-Maccabean parallel); ACTS 12:23 (Herod Agrippa I 'eaten of worms'); 2 SAMUEL 17:23 (Ahithophel's death by self-hanging); 1 SAMUEL 25:38 ('the LORD smote Nabal, that he died' — ten days after his stroke); ISAIAH 14:11 ('the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee' — Lucifer's-fall-into-Sheol). The disgusting-death-of-the-proud-tyrant motif functions rhetorically as DIVINE-POETIC-JUSTICE: the tyrant who consumed others is now consumed; the body-that-killed-others is dissolved by worms; the proud-flesh is humiliated. Meqabyan's distinctive feature: Ṣiruṣaydan's foul-death CLOSES THE TRILOGY'S PRINCIPAL VILLAIN-ARC that has run from 1 Mq Ch 1 through 2 Mq Ch 12, the MOST EXTENDED SUSTAINED-VILLAIN narrative in the Meqabyan corpus.

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) Second Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan II) (c. 600 AD)

DEATH OF ṢIRUṢAYDAN — narrative climax of the trilogy's PRINCIPAL VILLAIN-ARC that has run from 1 Mq Ch. 1 through 2 Mq Ch. 12 (the MOST EXTENDED SUSTAINED-VILLAIN narrative in the Meqabyan corpus). Ṣiruṣaydan's death pattern echoes the divine-judgment-on-prideful-kings tradition: Nebuchadnezzar at Daniel 4:31-37 (driven to graze like an ox) + Herod at Acts 12:23 (eaten by worms) + Antiochus IV at 2 Maccabees 9 (worm-infested + foul-smelling demise). Per Horovitz 1905 + Dillmann Lexicon Linguae Aethiopicae (1865): Ṣiruṣaydan etymology connects to TYRE + SIDON (Ṣiru + Ṣaydan), the Phoenician-coastal cities + canonical-type for arrogant maritime-commercial power (Ezekiel 26-28 prophecies). The villain-name is itself a TYPOLOGICAL CIPHER rather than historical-king identification.

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) Second Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan II) (c. 600 AD)

ṢIRUṢAYDAN'S FOUL-SMELLING DEMISE — the proud-tyrant-pestilence-death topos (paired with seed 12:11 villain-arc climax). The death-by-foul-disease pattern parallels: 2 MACCABEES 9:5-12 (Antiochus IV's worm-infested-and-foul-smelling demise — the canonical-LXX-Maccabean parallel); ACTS 12:23 (Herod Agrippa I 'eaten of worms'); 2 SAMUEL 17:23 (Ahithophel's death by self-hanging); 1 SAMUEL 25:38 ('the LORD smote Nabal, that he died' — ten days after his stroke); ISAIAH 14:11 ('the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee' — Lucifer's-fall-into-Sheol). The disgusting-death-of-the-proud-tyrant motif functions rhetorically as DIVINE-POETIC-JUSTICE: the tyrant who consumed others is now consumed; the body-that-killed-others is dissolved by worms; the proud-flesh is humiliated. Meqabyan's distinctive feature: Ṣiruṣaydan's foul-death CLOSES THE TRILOGY'S PRINCIPAL VILLAIN-ARC that has run from 1 Mq Ch 1 through 2 Mq Ch 12, the MOST EXTENDED SUSTAINED-VILLAIN narrative in the Meqabyan corpus.
